Hi Emily — great conversation this morning. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our side so we keep momentum: 

Recap (what we heard)
- Primary use case: automated patient-summary generation from structured EHR + clinical notes (low-latency, high-precision fields required).
- Output must conform to an existing patient_summary JSON schema (strict types, enums for diagnosis codes, max tokens per field).
- Volume: ~1k summaries/day with 95% under 500ms generation SLA for interactive clinician UI.
- Data sensitivity: PHI-regulated; HealthCore prefers private deployment options but will consider dedicated first.

Immediate asks / proposed deliverables
1) Technical proposal (model choices + benchmark snapshot) — Rishi to send a recommended short-list and tradeoffs.
2) JSON schema conformance plan + sample schema — we attached the schema you shared and will run structured-output evals. (Attachment: patient_schema_v1.json)
3) Prompt set and benchmark harness — we’ll share a Drive folder with the prompt suite and per-prompt pass/fail criteria.
4) Hands-on eval/session — propose Wed 11/24 or Thu 11/25 for a 60-min technical walkthrough and live eval.

Attachments: discovery_notes_20261121.pdf (notes from today's call)

Next action: Rishi will send model recommendations and a short benchmark summary by EOD Monday. I’ll follow up with calendar invites for the live eval session.

Thanks again — excited to dig in.

- The patient_summary schema is strict about code enums and date formats; any generated field outside the allowed enums will trigger downstream validation failures in our pipeline.
- For the SLA: 95% < 500ms is the target for interactive UI; batch runs can be slower.
- Security: we'll need an outline of your private deployment footprint and KMS options before we share a small redacted sample dataset for benchmarking.

Can Rishi include a recommended approach for guaranteeing JSON schema compliance (validation + guardrail prompts vs. model-constrained generation)? Also please include a note on retry/backoff behavior if the model returns malformed JSON.

Subject: Re: Discovery follow-up: model recommendations, JSON schema conformance, and next steps

Hi Emily — quick technical note and recommended starting point based on the constraints you shared. Long answer below; TL;DR at top.

TL;DR
- Recommended models: Redwood-curated Llama-3-70B (quant-8) for best structured-output fidelity at moderate cost; Llama-3-13B quant-4 for lower-cost screening; fallback: Llama-2-70B fp16 on dedicated infra for max-quality.
- Strategy for JSON conformance: produce 'raw' JSON from model + deterministic post-processor validator step that corrects predictable enum/format issues; enforce hard rejection for critical fields and surface repair suggestions.
- Retry/backoff: deterministic retry up to 2 attempts with progressive prompt tightening (schema hinting and example-driven correction); if still invalid — fall back to constrained template fill or flag for human review.

Why these models?
- L3-70B q8: strong zero-shot structured-output abilities with our structured decoding tweaks and temperature=0.0 defaults. Latency estimate (dedicated gpus + optimized kernels): median token RT 45ms; median end-to-end for a ~200-token summary ~280–350ms.
- L3-13B q4: good for high-throughput pre-filtering where occasional manual review is acceptable. Lower cost by ~3–4x.

JSON conformance approach (recommended, pragmatic)
1) Prompt scaffolding: call out schema, required fields, allowed enums, and a small set of 3 positive/negative examples in few-shot.
2) Structured output enforcement: request a JSON object only, add a top-level wrapper like {"redwood_schema_v": "1.0", "payload": { ... }} to simplify parsing.
3) Post-processor validate/repair: run a fast JSON schema validator server-side; attempt deterministic repairs (e.g., enum mapping, date canonicalization). If repair changes > 10% of fields or critical required fields remain invalid, fail and surface to UI.
4) Observability: log both raw and repaired outputs with a diff score for quality monitoring.

Retry/backoff policy - First attempt: base prompt (as above) + sampling temp 0.0.
- If invalid JSON: retry 1 — tighten prompt (explicit 'return valid JSON' and include corrected example).
- Retry 2: switch to deterministic decoding + increase system instruction strictness.
- After Retry 2: route to constrained template filler or human-in-the-loop.

Benchmarks and artifacts
- Snapshot results: see attached CSV for our initial pass on your prompt set (redwood_benchmarks_healthcare_eval_20261120.csv). Summary: L3-70B q8 achieved 92% strict-schema pass rate on the 120-sample prompt set, median latency (opt kernels) 320ms. L3-13B q4 achieved 75% pass rate but 3x lower cost.
- Prompt suite and longer benchmark prompts: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1a2b3c_healthcore_prompt_suite
- Attached: patient_schema_v1.json (we used this as the validator input).

Operational notes
- KMS: Redwood Private supports customer KMS via AWS KMS or HashiCorp Vault (bring-your-own).
- Deployment path: quick Dedicated PoC (2–4 weeks) to hit SLAs and then Private deployment for PHI if required.

Next steps I’ll do before the call on Thu:
- Drop a short runbook for schema conformance + a sample repair map for common enums.
- Share a short script to replay 50 representative prompts against L3-70B q8 in our sandbox so you can review raw vs repaired outputs.

Attachment: redwood_benchmarks_healthcare_eval_20261120.csv, patient_schema_v1.json

Happy to discuss further on Thu 11/25 10:00 PT.

—Rishi
